sites.name: Masjid Al-Haram
sites.shortDescription: The holiest mosque in Islam, surrounding the Kaaba in Mecca.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid Al-Haram is the largest mosque in the world and surrounds one of Islam's holiest sites, the Kaaba. Located in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, it is the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage and Umrah. Muslims around the world face toward the Kaaba during their daily prayers. The mosque has been expanded numerous times throughout history and can accommodate millions of worshippers simultaneously. Its current structure features massive minarets, grand archways, and the iconic clock tower complex.
sites.significance: The holiest site in Islam; direction of prayer (Qibla) for 1.8 billion Muslims worldwide

sites.name: Masjid An-Nabawi
sites.shortDescription: The Prophet's Mosque in Medina, built by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
sites.fullDescription: Masjid An-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque, was built by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) in 622 CE in Medina. It is the second holiest site in Islam after Masjid Al-Haram. The mosque contains the tomb of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), making it a site of immense spiritual significance. The iconic Green Dome marks the resting place of the Prophet. Over the centuries, the mosque has been expanded by various caliphs and sultans, and today it can accommodate over one million worshippers. It features beautiful calligraphy, retractable umbrellas in the courtyard, and the famous Riyad al-Jannah garden.
sites.significance: Second holiest site in Islam; resting place of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)

sites.name: Masjid Al-Aqsa
sites.shortDescription: The third holiest mosque in Islam, located on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid Al-Aqsa, meaning 'the farthest mosque', is the third holiest site in Islam. Located in the Old City of Jerusalem, it holds immense religious significance as the site to which Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) made his night journey (Isra) and from which he ascended to the heavens (Miraj). The compound, known as Haram al-Sharif, also includes the Dome of the Rock with its magnificent golden dome. The mosque has been a center of Islamic civilization and scholarship for over 1,400 years. It was the first Qibla (direction of prayer) for early Muslims.
sites.significance: Third holiest site in Islam; destination of Prophet's Night Journey (Isra wal Miraj)
sites.architecturalStyle: Early Islamic, Umayyad, Crusader modifications, Ayyubid

sites.name: Dome of the Rock
sites.shortDescription: An Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount with its iconic golden dome.
sites.fullDescription: The Dome of the Rock is an Islamic shrine located on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, built by Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan in 691-692 CE. It is one of the oldest extant works of Islamic architecture. The shrine's golden dome is one of the most recognizable images in the world. It was built over the Foundation Stone, which holds profound significance in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions. The interior features stunning Byzantine and early Islamic mosaics, intricate geometric patterns, and Quranic inscriptions.
sites.significance: One of oldest Islamic monuments; marks site of Prophet's ascension to heavens

sites.name: Hagia Sophia
sites.shortDescription: A magnificent structure in Istanbul converted to a mosque under Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II.
sites.fullDescription: Hagia Sophia (Ayasofya) is a magnificent architectural wonder in Istanbul, Turkey. Originally built as a Christian cathedral in 537 CE, it was converted to a mosque after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 CE by Sultan Mehmed II. The building served as the principal mosque of Istanbul for nearly 500 years. It became a museum in 1934 but was reconverted to a mosque in 2020. The structure is famous for its massive dome, stunning Byzantine mosaics, and grand interior. It represents a unique architectural heritage spanning Byzantine and Ottoman Islamic traditions.
sites.significance: Symbol of Ottoman triumph; architectural marvel blending Byzantine and Islamic heritage

sites.name: Blue Mosque
sites.shortDescription: Sultan Ahmed Mosque, famous for its six minarets and blue Iznik tiles.
sites.fullDescription: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque, popularly known as the Blue Mosque due to the blue Iznik tiles adorning its interior, was built between 1609 and 1616 CE during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I. Located in Istanbul, it is famous for its six minarets — an unusual number that caused controversy as it matched the minarets of the mosque in Mecca. The mosque features a cascade of domes and semi-domes, and its grand interior is decorated with over 20,000 hand-painted blue and white Iznik tiles. It remains an active mosque and one of Istanbul's most iconic landmarks.
sites.significance: Masterpiece of Ottoman architecture; famous for unique six minarets and blue Iznik tile interior

sites.name: Great Mosque of Cordoba
sites.shortDescription: The Mezquita, a stunning example of Moorish architecture in southern Spain.
sites.fullDescription: The Great Mosque of Cordoba (Mezquita) is one of the finest examples of Moorish architecture in the world, located in Cordoba, Spain. Built during the Umayyad Caliphate of Cordoba beginning in 784 CE, it was expanded by subsequent rulers over two centuries. The mosque features the iconic forest of columns with distinctive red-and-white striped arches, intricate geometric mosaics, and a spectacular mihrab. During the height of Islamic Spain (Al-Andalus), Cordoba was one of the most advanced cities in Europe, and this mosque was its crown jewel. A cathedral was later built within the mosque during the Spanish Reconquista.
sites.significance: Crown jewel of Al-Andalus Islamic civilization; UNESCO World Heritage Site

sites.name: Alhambra Palace
sites.shortDescription: The jewel of Islamic palatial architecture in Granada, Spain.
sites.fullDescription: The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex located in Granada, Spain, built during the Nasrid dynasty in the 13th-14th centuries CE. It represents the pinnacle of Islamic palatial architecture in Western Europe and is considered one of the finest examples of Islamic art and architecture in existence. The palace complex features stunning geometric tilework, intricate muqarnas (honeycomb vaulting), elegant courtyards with reflecting pools, lush gardens, and delicate stucco arabesques. The Court of the Lions with its famous marble fountain is among the most celebrated spaces in Islamic architecture.
sites.significance: Pinnacle of Nasrid Islamic architecture; UNESCO World Heritage Site; last great Islamic kingdom in Spain

sites.name: Imam Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A masterpiece of Safavid Islamic architecture in Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square.
sites.fullDescription: The Imam Mosque (formerly Shah Mosque) in Isfahan, Iran, is widely considered one of the most beautiful mosques in the world and a supreme achievement of Persian Islamic architecture. Built during the Safavid dynasty under Shah Abbas I between 1611 and 1629 CE, it stands on the southern side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The mosque is famous for its resplendent tiled facade, massive portal, twin minarets, and a spectacular main dome covered in mosaic faience tilework in shades of blue, turquoise, and gold. The acoustic properties of the main dome are extraordinary.
sites.significance: Masterpiece of Safavid Persian Islamic art; UNESCO World Heritage Site

sites.name: Badshahi Mosque
sites.shortDescription: One of the world's largest mosques, a Mughal masterpiece in Lahore.
sites.fullDescription: The Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, Pakistan, is one of the most iconic examples of Mughal architecture. Built by the sixth Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb between 1671 and 1673 CE, it was the world's largest mosque for over three centuries. The mosque features a grand red sandstone exterior with white marble domes and minarets, beautiful geometric patterns, and exquisite marble inlay work. The main prayer hall can accommodate 10,000 worshippers, while the courtyard can hold up to 95,000. The mosque stands as a testament to the grandeur of the Mughal Empire at its zenith.
sites.significance: Greatest Mughal architectural achievement; symbol of Lahore and Pakistan

sites.name: Jama Masjid Delhi
sites.shortDescription: India's largest mosque, built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan.
sites.fullDescription: The Jama Masjid of Delhi is India's largest mosque and one of the most magnificent examples of Mughal architecture. Commissioned by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan and completed in 1656 CE, it was built with red sandstone and white marble. The mosque features three great gates, four towers, and two 40-metre minarets. The courtyard can hold over 25,000 worshippers. The mosque's name means 'World-Reflecting Mosque.' Shah Jahan also built the Taj Mahal, and the Jama Masjid shares similar architectural elements with that iconic monument.
sites.significance: India's largest mosque; finest example of Mughal religious architecture

sites.name: Kairouan Great Mosque
sites.shortDescription: One of the oldest and most important mosques in North Africa.
sites.fullDescription: The Great Mosque of Kairouan, also known as the Mosque of Uqba, is one of the oldest and most prestigious mosques in the Islamic world. Founded in 670 CE by the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, it is considered the fourth holiest site in Islam and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The mosque served as a model for later Islamic architecture in the western Mediterranean. Its square minaret is considered the oldest surviving minaret in the world. The mosque's prayer hall features a forest of columns, many reused from ancient Roman and Byzantine structures. Kairouan was a major center of Islamic learning in the early centuries of Islam.
sites.significance: Fourth holiest site in Islam; oldest mosque in North Africa; mother of North African mosques

sites.name: Djinguereber Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A 14th-century mosque in Timbuktu, built using traditional Sudano-Sahelian architecture.
sites.fullDescription: The Djinguereber Mosque is a famous and historic mosque in Timbuktu, Mali, built in 1327 CE. It was commissioned by Mansa Musa, the immensely wealthy Emperor of the Mali Empire, following his return from Hajj to Mecca. The mosque was designed by the Andalusian poet and architect Abou Es Haq Es Saheli. Built in the traditional Sudano-Sahelian architectural style using mud bricks and timber, it can accommodate 2,000 worshippers. Timbuktu was once a great center of Islamic learning, and the mosque is part of the city's UNESCO World Heritage designation.
sites.significance: Built by Mansa Musa after his legendary Hajj; center of medieval Sub-Saharan Islamic learning

sites.name: Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque
sites.shortDescription: Oman's grand national mosque, featuring the world's largest hand-woven carpet.
sites.fullDescription: The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque in Muscat, Oman, is one of the most impressive mosques in the world. Built between 1995 and 2001 CE, it was a gift from Sultan Qaboos bin Said Al Said to the people of Oman. The mosque can accommodate 20,000 worshippers. It is famous for housing the world's largest hand-woven carpet, measuring 4,343 square meters and weighing 21 tons, and one of the world's largest chandeliers. The prayer hall features a stunning interior dome and intricate Islamic geometric patterns. The mosque welcomes non-Muslim visitors and serves as a symbol of Oman's Islamic identity.
sites.significance: Symbol of Oman's Islamic heritage; houses world's largest hand-woven carpet

sites.name: Da Tok Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A historic brick mosque in Pattani, southern Thailand, restored by the governor of Yaring.
sites.fullDescription: Da Tok Mosque (MAHS-THA-PTN-YAR-LMP-S-001-F-0001) stands south of Makam Tok Payang within a densely populated village, surrounded closely by houses. The complex includes a renovated mosque building and a large graveyard, each enclosed by separate walls. Once dilapidated and abandoned, the mosque was later restored and enlarged by Phraya Phiphit Senamat, governor of Yaring. Built of brick, plastered with lime, and painted white, it has a rectangular west-facing plan, balconies, colored glass windows, a dome, spiral staircase, and eastern extension.
sites.significance: A culturally significant mosque in the Muslim heartland of southern Thailand, representing the blend of Malay-Islamic and colonial architectural traditions.

sites.name: Masjid al-Qiblatayn
sites.shortDescription: The Mosque of the Two Qiblas — where the direction of prayer was divinely changed from Jerusalem to Mecca.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid al-Qiblatayn, meaning the Mosque of the Two Qiblas, stands as one of the most historically significant mosques in Islam. It was here, during the second year of Hijra (623 CE), that the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) received the divine revelation commanding the change of the qibla — the direction of prayer — from Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem to the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca. According to tradition, the Prophet was leading the Dhuhr (midday) prayer when the revelation descended, and he pivoted mid-prayer to face the new direction. The congregation turned with him, marking a defining moment in Islamic worship. The original structure was modest, but the mosque has been expanded and renovated multiple times, most extensively by the Saudi government in 1987. Today it stands as a radiant white marble structure adorned with two mihrab niches — one facing Jerusalem and one facing Mecca — symbolising the historic transition.
sites.significance: The only mosque in Islamic history where the qibla changed mid-prayer, marking the shift in the direction of prayer from Jerusalem to Mecca as commanded by divine revelation.
sites.architecturalStyle: Contemporary Islamic — white marble with twin minarets and dual mihrabs

sites.name: Al-Azhar Mosque
sites.shortDescription: One of Islam's oldest universities and the world's pre-eminent centre of Sunni Islamic scholarship.
sites.fullDescription: Founded in 970 CE by the Fatimid dynasty, Al-Azhar Mosque in Cairo is among the oldest continually operating universities in the world. Its name means "The Resplendent" and it serves as the global reference point for Sunni Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and Arabic language. The mosque's multi-period architecture reflects a thousand years of patronage from successive dynasties — Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk, and Ottoman — each leaving distinctive minarets and gateways. Al-Azhar University, attached to the mosque, draws students from over 100 countries and issues scholarly opinions (fatwas) followed by millions globally.
sites.significance: The most influential centre of Sunni Islamic learning; home of Al-Azhar University whose scholars have shaped Islamic thought for over 1,000 years

sites.name: Faisal Mosque
sites.shortDescription: The iconic shell-shaped national mosque of Pakistan in Islamabad, one of the largest mosques in the world.
sites.fullDescription: Faisal Mosque is the national mosque of Pakistan, located in Islamabad at the foot of the Margalla Hills. It was designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay and funded by King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz of Saudi Arabia, after whom it is named. Construction began in 1976 and was completed in 1986. The mosque departs radically from traditional domed mosque architecture — its prayer hall is shaped like a Bedouin tent and flanked by four soaring minarets, creating a silhouette unlike any other mosque in the world. The main prayer hall can accommodate up to 74,000 worshippers inside, with the surrounding grounds holding an additional 200,000. It served as the largest mosque in the world from 1986 to 1993.
sites.significance: National mosque of Pakistan and an icon of contemporary Islamic architecture, blending Mughal heritage with modernist design.

sites.name: Katara Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A stunning modern mosque in the Katara Cultural Village of Doha, blending Andalusian and Levantine Islamic aesthetics.
sites.fullDescription: The Katara Mosque, also known as the Grand Mosque of Katara, is set within the Katara Cultural Village on the shores of Doha, Qatar. Completed around 2010, the mosque reflects a synthesis of Andalusian, Ottoman, and Levantine architectural traditions — featuring a grand central dome, intricate geometric tilework, colonnaded arcades, and a single elegant minaret. It serves the cultural village community and visitors as both a place of worship and an architectural landmark. The exterior is clad in blue and white Andalusian-inspired faience tiles, while the interior features hand-painted ceilings, marble floors, and delicate arabesque carvings. The mosque is surrounded by a large courtyard with fountains and shaded walkways.
sites.significance: A landmark of contemporary Islamic architecture in Qatar, representing the country's commitment to preserving Islamic cultural heritage within a modern context.

sites.name: Shah Rukn-e-Alam Shrine
sites.shortDescription: The magnificent 14th-century Sufi shrine of Saint Rukn-ud-Din Abul Fatah in Multan, a masterpiece of Tughluq architecture.
sites.fullDescription: The Shrine of Shah Rukn-e-Alam in Multan, Pakistan, is one of the most magnificent examples of early Islamic monumental architecture in South Asia. Built between 1320 and 1324 CE during the Tughluq dynasty, it was constructed by Sultan Ghiyath ud-Din Tughluq as his own mausoleum but later given to the Sufi saint Rukn-ud-Din Abul Fatah (1251–1335 CE), who was a prominent figure of the Suhrawardiyya Sufi order. The shrine stands on a high octagonal base and is crowned with a massive dome. The exterior walls are decorated with elaborate geometric patterns in blue, white, and terracotta glazed tiles interspersed with carved woodwork. The main chamber contains the saint's tomb and is perpetually visited by devoted pilgrims. The shrine dominates the skyline of Multan and is considered the jewel of the city.
sites.significance: One of the holiest Sufi shrines in Pakistan and a supreme example of Tughluq-era monumental Islamic architecture in the subcontinent.

sites.name: Miqat Al-Sail Al-Kabeer
sites.shortDescription: The miqat for pilgrims approaching Makkah from the direction of Najd and Ta'if, where ihram is assumed before entering the sacred precincts.
sites.fullDescription: Miqat Al-Sail Al-Kabeer, also known as Qarn al-Manazil, is one of the five sacred boundary points (mawaqit) established by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for Hajj and Umrah. It is located approximately 80 km east of Makkah on the road from Ta'if, serving pilgrims arriving from Najd (central Arabia), the Arabian Gulf states, and travellers from the east. The miqat marks the boundary beyond which no Muslim intending to perform Hajj or Umrah may pass without entering the state of ihram — donning the white unsewn garments and making the intention (niyyah). The site today features a large mosque complex with ablution facilities, where pilgrims stop, change into ihram, and recite the talbiyah before continuing toward the Haram. The location corresponds to the wadi of Al-Sail Al-Kabeer, and is referenced in authenticated hadiths of the Prophet ﷺ.
sites.significance: One of the five prophetically designated miqat boundary points for Hajj and Umrah; the entry point for all pilgrims arriving from Najd and the east.

sites.name: Shrine of Imam Ali
sites.shortDescription: The golden-domed mausoleum of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib in Najaf, one of the holiest sites in Islam.
sites.fullDescription: The Shrine of Imam Ali (also known as the Imam Ali Mosque or the Holy Shrine of Ali ibn Abi Talib) is located in Najaf, Iraq, and marks the burial place of Ali ibn Abi Talib — cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the fourth Caliph of Islam. The shrine is among the holiest sites in Islam, drawing millions of pilgrims annually. The current structure dates largely from the Buyid, Safavid, and later periods, featuring a magnificent golden dome, gilded minarets, and vast iwan halls adorned with intricate mirror mosaic work (āina-kāri). The shrine complex is adjacent to Wadi Al-Salam, the largest cemetery in the world, where millions of Muslims seek to be buried near the Imam. Major expansions were carried out under the Safavid Shahs and in the 20th and 21st centuries.
sites.significance: One of the holiest sites in Islam, marking the burial place of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib; a supreme pilgrimage destination for Muslims worldwide.

sites.name: Miqat Dhul Hulaifah
sites.shortDescription: The farthest miqat from Makkah, located near Madinah and designated for pilgrims travelling from al-Madinah al-Munawwarah.
sites.fullDescription: Miqat Dhul Hulaifah, popularly known as Abyar Ali (Bir Ali), is the miqat designated by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for pilgrims setting out toward Makkah from the direction of al-Madinah al-Munawwarah. It is located approximately 9 km south of Madinah and is the farthest of the five mawaqit from the Kaaba (about 450 km). It is the miqat used by the Prophet ﷺ himself when he departed from Madinah for both the Farewell Pilgrimage and for Umrah. The site features Masjid Al-Shajarah (Mosque of the Tree), named after a large tree under which it is narrated the Prophet ﷺ rested. Today it is a large, modern mosque complex accommodating tens of thousands of pilgrims who stop here to change into ihram, perform ablution, make the intention of Hajj or Umrah, and recite the talbiyah before departing for Makkah.
sites.significance: The miqat used by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself; the farthest miqat from Makkah and the one designated for pilgrims from Madinah.

sites.name: Miqat Al-Juhfah
sites.shortDescription: The ancient miqat near Rabigh designated for pilgrims approaching Makkah from the north and west — from Syria, Egypt, and North Africa.
sites.fullDescription: Miqat Al-Juhfah is one of the five mawaqit designated by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for the assumption of ihram before entering the Haram of Makkah. It is located near the modern town of Rabigh on the Red Sea coast, approximately 183 km northwest of Makkah. Historically, Al-Juhfah was a settlement on the ancient pilgrimage route from Syria and Egypt; after it fell into ruin, the nearby town of Rabigh became the practical miqat point. The miqat serves pilgrims arriving from Syria, Jordan, Egypt, North Africa, and the Levant. The site today features a large mosque (Masjid Al-Juhfah or Masjid Miqat Rabigh) where pilgrims perform ghusl, don ihram garments, and recite the talbiyah.
sites.significance: The prophetically designated miqat for pilgrims from the Levant, Egypt, and North Africa; one of the five permanent boundary stations for Hajj and Umrah.

sites.name: Masjid Quba
sites.shortDescription: The first mosque ever built in Islam, established by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ upon his arrival in Madinah in 622 CE.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid Quba is the first mosque constructed in Islamic history. When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived in Madinah after the Hijra from Makkah in 622 CE, the first thing he did was lay the foundation of this mosque in the settlement of Quba on the outskirts of the city. He himself participated in carrying stones for its construction. The original structure was modest, but the mosque has been rebuilt and expanded multiple times — most recently in 1986 with a major Saudi renovation giving it its current form: gleaming white domes, four tall minarets, and spacious courtyards. The Prophet ﷺ stated that the reward of praying two rak'ahs in Masjid Quba is equivalent to performing one Umrah, making it one of the most spiritually significant mosques in Islam. It is located approximately 5 km south of Masjid An-Nabawi.
sites.significance: The first mosque ever built in Islam, founded by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself; praying two rak'ahs here carries the reward of a complete Umrah.

sites.name: Mount Arafat
sites.shortDescription: The sacred plain 20 km from Makkah where the Standing (Wuquf) — the essential rite of Hajj — takes place on 9 Dhul Hijjah.
sites.fullDescription: Mount Arafat (Jabal Arafat), also called Jabal al-Rahmah (Mountain of Mercy), is a granite hill and surrounding plain approximately 20 km east of Makkah al-Mukarramah. It is the most essential site of the Hajj pilgrimage — the Prophet ﷺ declared: ""Hajj is Arafat."" Every year on 9 Dhul Hijjah, more than two million pilgrims gather on the plain from noon to sunset in supplication, dhikr, and repentance before Allah — a gathering described as a foretaste of the Day of Judgment. It was here that the Prophet ﷺ delivered his historic Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada) in 632 CE. It is also the site where the final verse of the Quran is believed to have been revealed: ""This day I have perfected for you your religion..."" (Quran 5:3). The Namirah Mosque on the western edge of the plain serves the millions of pilgrims who congregate there annually.
sites.significance: The pivotal site of Hajj — standing here on 9 Dhul Hijjah is the essential pillar of the pilgrimage; the Prophet ﷺ declared "Hajj is Arafat."

sites.name: Sultan Salahuddin Abdul Aziz Shah Mosque
sites.arabicName: مسجد السلطان صلاح الدين عبد العزيز شاه
sites.shortDescription: The largest mosque in Malaysia, known as the Blue Mosque for its iconic blue and silver dome.
sites.fullDescription: The Sultan Salahuddin Abdul Aziz Shah Mosque, commonly known as the Blue Mosque, is the state mosque of Selangor and the largest mosque in Malaysia. Situated on a 35-acre hilltop in Shah Alam, it was commissioned by Sultan Salahuddin Abdul Aziz Shah when he declared Shah Alam the capital of Selangor in 1974. Construction began in 1982 and was completed in 1988. The mosque features one of the world's largest religious domes at 51.2 metres in diameter, clad in blue and silver panels. Its four minarets stand 142.3 metres tall, once ranking among the world's tallest. The interior includes fine Arabic calligraphy by Egyptian calligrapher Sheikh Abdel Moneim Mohamed Ali El Sharkawi, blue stained glass windows, and a timber ceiling in a crisscrossing pattern. The design blends Malay and Modernist Islamic architecture. It overlooks the Garden of Islamic Arts, a landscaped park inspired by the Quranic Garden of Paradise.
sites.significance: Largest mosque in Malaysia; second largest in Southeast Asia; iconic Blue Mosque of Malaysia

sites.name: Great Mosque of Tirana
sites.shortDescription: The largest mosque in the Balkans, opened in 2024 in central Tirana.
sites.fullDescription: The Great Mosque of Tirana, also known as the Namazgah Mosque, is the largest mosque in the Balkans. Located in central Tirana near Skanderbeg Square, its foundation stone was laid in 1992 and construction began in 2015. Officially opened on 10 October 2024, the mosque was designed by Turkish architect Muharrem Hilmi Senalp in a Classical Ottoman style inspired by Istanbul's Blue Mosque. It features four 50-metre minarets and a 30-metre central dome. With a capacity of 10,000 worshippers (8,000 inside, 2,000 outside), it serves as both a religious centre and a cultural hub, including a Museum of Coexistence that celebrates Albania's tradition of religious harmony. The mosque was built adjacent to the Catholic and Orthodox cathedrals, deliberately forming a triangle representing interfaith coexistence.
sites.significance: Largest mosque in the Balkans; symbol of Albanian religious harmony and interfaith coexistence

sites.name: Afsonalar Vodiysi Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A modern mosque within the Valley of Legends cultural park in Namangan, Uzbekistan, celebrated for its striking Central Asian Islamic architecture.
sites.fullDescription: The Afsonalar Vodiysi Mosque, also known as the Yusufxon o'g'li Qosimxon Mosque, is situated within the Valley of Legends (Afsonalar Vodiysi) cultural and recreational park in Namangan, the second-largest city in Uzbekistan's Fergana Valley. The mosque serves as both a spiritual centre and an architectural landmark, blending modern construction techniques with traditional Central Asian Islamic design motifs. Its prominent dome and minaret reflect the Timurid architectural heritage of the region, while the surrounding parkland provides a serene setting that draws visitors from across the Fergana Valley. The mosque stands as a symbol of Uzbekistan's post-independence cultural renaissance, representing the renewed commitment to Islamic heritage in Central Asia following the Soviet era.
sites.significance: A significant modern mosque in Central Asia representing Uzbekistan's cultural revival and Islamic architectural heritage in the Fergana Valley.

sites.name: Kudhu Miskiyy
sites.shortDescription: An abandoned traditional mosque on Kondey island in Gaafu Alifu Atoll, Maldives, built by descendants of the master builders of Male's Old Friday Mosque.
sites.fullDescription: The Kudhu Miskiyy is a traditional Maldivian mosque located on Kondey island in Gaafu Alifu Atoll (North Huvadhu), in the southern reaches of the Maldives archipelago. According to local oral history, the mosque was built by Ali and Mahmud Maavadi Kaleyfaan, skilled craftsmen from Kondey who had earlier helped construct the famous Hukuru Miskiyy (Old Friday Mosque) in Male, the capital. After completing their work in Male, they returned to their home island and built this mosque with the remaining materials. The mosque has since been expanded beyond its original footprint, though elements of the older structure remain visible from the back. Today it stands abandoned, a silent witness to the maritime Islamic heritage of the Maldivian atolls and the once-flourishing tradition of coral-stone mosque building that defined the nation's architectural identity.
sites.significance: A rare surviving example of traditional Maldivian mosque architecture in the outer atolls, linked by oral tradition to the master builders of Male's UNESCO-listed Old Friday Mosque.

sites.name: Ban Tok Chao Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A distinctive mosque in Surat Thani, Thailand, originally constructed on wooden stilts with a no-longer-used upper-floor prayer hall, later converted in 2014 to its current form.
sites.fullDescription: The Ban Tok Chao Mosque in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, is a remarkable example of syncretic Islamic architecture that blends Malay-Muslim, Thai Buddhist, and Arabian artistic traditions. The mosque was originally built entirely on wooden stilts, a construction technique common in the wetland and coastal regions of southern Thailand. Its upper floor once served as the prayer hall, but is no longer in use. In 2014, a brick wall was erected around the ground floor — the existing stilt locks are still visible — and the ground level was converted into the present prayer hall. The roof carries a unique Muslim-style decorative scheme characteristic of southern Thai mosques: the gables bear paintings of Garuda, the mythical bird and national emblem of Thailand; Al-Buraq, the winged horse-like creature from Islamic tradition that carried the Prophet Muhammad on his Night Journey; and a female face adorned in an Arabic-style hijab. This extraordinary combination of symbols reflects the deep intercultural history of Islam in Thailand, where Malay-Muslim communities have long coexisted within a predominantly Buddhist kingdom, producing architecture that speaks in multiple visual languages simultaneously.
sites.significance: A rare surviving example of stilt-based mosque architecture in Southeast Asia, with uniquely syncretic decorative art blending Thai, Islamic, and Malay visual traditions.

sites.name: Al Mohamadi Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A historic mosque in the Habous district of Casablanca, Morocco, commissioned by King Mohammed V, exemplifying early 20th-century Moroccan colonial-era Islamic architecture.
sites.fullDescription: The Al Mohamadi Mosque stands in the Habous district (New Medina) of Casablanca, a neighbourhood built during the French Protectorate era to accommodate the growing Moroccan population. Commissioned by King Mohammed V of Morocco, the mosque reflects the distinctive architectural synthesis of that period — blending traditional Moroccan Islamic elements such as horseshoe arches, zellige tilework, and carved stucco with the urban planning sensibilities of early 20th-century Casablanca. The Habous district itself is renowned for its orderly streets, artisan workshops, and bustling souks, and the mosque serves as both a spiritual anchor and a historical marker of Morocco's path toward independence. As one of the landmark mosques commissioned by the beloved monarch who would later lead the nation to independence, the Al Mohamadi Mosque holds a special place in the collective memory of Casablanca's residents.
sites.significance: Commissioned by King Mohammed V, a symbol of Moroccan national identity and the colonial-era architectural heritage of Casablanca's Habous district.

sites.name: White Mosque
sites.shortDescription: A striking modern mosque at the Bolgar Historical and Archaeological Complex in Tatarstan, Russia, built to commemorate the region's Islamic heritage and Volga Bulgar history.
sites.fullDescription: The White Mosque stands at the Bolgar Historical and Archaeological Complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the banks of the Volga River in the Republic of Tatarstan, Russia. This modern mosque was constructed to honour the region's profound Islamic heritage as the centre of the Volga Bulgaria, one of the earliest Islamic states in Eastern Europe, which adopted Islam in 922 CE under Khan Almish. The mosque's pristine white architecture stands in deliberate contrast to the ancient ruins of Bolgar that surround it — the remains of the medieval capital of the Volga Bulgars, a Turkic people who played a pivotal role in the Islamisation of the Eurasian steppe. The Bolgar complex, known as the 'northern Mecca' in Russian Muslim tradition, attracts pilgrims and visitors who come to connect with this early chapter of Islamic civilisation in Eastern Europe. The White Mosque serves as a living prayer space and a powerful symbol of the continuity of Islamic faith in the Volga region, bridging the medieval past of the Bolgar Khanate with the vibrant Muslim community of modern Tatarstan.
sites.significance: Part of the Bolgar UNESCO World Heritage Site; commemorates the 922 CE adoption of Islam by the Volga Bulgars, one of the earliest Islamic states in Eastern Europe.

sites.name: Mina
sites.shortDescription: A valley six kilometres east of Masjid al-Haram in Makkah, known as the Tent City of Hajj.
sites.fullDescription: Mina (Arabic: منى) is a valley six kilometres east of the Masjid al-Haram in Makkah. It is where Hajj pilgrims sleep overnight on the 8th, 11th, 12th (and some even on the 13th) of Dhul Hijjah. The valley of Mina contains the Jamarat, the three stone pillars which are pelted by pilgrims as part of the rituals of Hajj. Mina is referenced in Surah Baqarah in the Quran: "And remember Allah during [specific] numbered days. Then whoever hastens [his departure] in two days – there is no sin upon him; and whoever delays [until the third] – there is no sin upon him – for him who fears Allah . And fear Allah and know that unto Him you will be gathered." [2:203]. The name Mina is derived from the root letters ma-na-ya which means "to be put to the test" or "to undergo" — connected to the test that Prophet Ebrahim (عليه السلام) had to undergo when he was ordered to sacrifice his son. When his resolve was proven, a ram was sacrificed in place. The word can also mean "to flow" because the blood of sacrificial animals flows here during Eidul Adha. Around 3 million pilgrims stay annually in Mina in more than 100,000 air-conditioned tents, leading to Mina also being known as the "Tent City". In this very spot the First Pledge by a group of 12 Men from Madinah was taken, marking the turning point and revolution of Yathrib which later became the luminous city of Madinah.
sites.significance: Essential Hajj pilgrimage site; home to the Jamarat and the famous Tent City accommodating millions of pilgrims

sites.name: Jamarat
sites.shortDescription: The three stone pillars in Mina that are stoned by pilgrims during the ritual of Rami al-Jamarat in Hajj.
sites.fullDescription: The Jamarat are three stone pillars situated in the valley of Mina, near Makkah, Saudi Arabia. They represent the locations where Prophet Ebrahim (عليه السلام) was tempted by Satan (Iblis) to disobey Allah's command to sacrifice his son, Ismail (عليه السلام). Each time Satan appeared, Prophet Ebrahim drove him away by throwing stones at him. The three pillars are known as Jamrat al-Ula (the first), Jamrat al-Wusta (the middle), and Jamrat al-Aqaba (the largest). During the days of Hajj (10th, 11th, and 12th of Dhul Hijjah), pilgrims perform the ritual of Rami al-Jamarat — symbolically stoning Satan and reaffirming their rejection of evil. The Jamarat Bridge, a multi-level pedestrian bridge, was constructed to safely accommodate the millions of pilgrims who perform this ritual. The largest pillar, Jamrat al-Aqaba, is stoned on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah (Yawm al-Nahr), while all three are stoned on the 11th and 12th. The ritual represents the triumph of faith and obedience to Allah over the whispers of temptation.
sites.significance: Sacred Hajj ritual site; symbol of resisting temptation and the triumph of faith over evil
sites.architecturalStyle: Ancient stone pillars with modern bridge infrastructure

sites.name: Masjid Nimrah
sites.shortDescription: The mosque in the plain of Arafat where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) delivered his Farewell Sermon during Hajj.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid Nimrah is situated on the plain of Arafat, approximately 20 kilometres east of Makkah, Saudi Arabia. It is one of the most significant mosques in the Islamic world due to its direct connection to the Hajj pilgrimage. On the 9th of Dhul Hijjah, the Day of Arafat, the imam of Masjid Nimrah delivers the Khutbah (sermon) of Wuquf — the standing at Arafat — and leads the combined Dhuhr and Asr prayers in congregation. This mirrors the practice of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), who delivered his historic Farewell Sermon at this very location during his final Hajj in 10 AH (632 CE), addressing over 100,000 companions. The sermon covered fundamental principles of Islam including the sanctity of life, property, and honour; the abolition of usury; the equality of all Muslims; and the rights of women. The current mosque structure was built to accommodate the vast number of pilgrims who gather here on the Day of Arafat, with modern facilities and a large prayer hall. It stands as a living monument to the final public address of the Prophet and the spiritual climax of the Hajj pilgrimage.
sites.significance: Site of the Prophet's Farewell Sermon; the khutbah and combined prayers of Wuquf at Arafat are performed here annually on the Day of Arafat

sites.name: Muzdalifah
sites.shortDescription: An open plain between Mina and Arafat where Hajj pilgrims spend the night after the Day of Arafat, collecting pebbles for the Jamarat ritual.
sites.fullDescription: Muzdalifah is an open plain situated between the plains of Mina and Arafat, approximately 8 kilometres from Mina and 7 kilometres from Arafat, in the Makkah region of Saudi Arabia. It is one of the most important locations in the Hajj pilgrimage, serving as the overnight resting place for pilgrims on the night of the 9th to the 10th of Dhul Hijjah — after the Day of Arafat (Wuquf) and before the ritual stoning at the Jamarat. Pilgrims arrive at Muzdalifah after sunset from Arafat, where they perform the combined Maghrib and Isha prayers. They spend the night under the open sky (or in tents), engaging in prayer, reflection, and rest. The most distinctive activity at Muzdalifah is the collection of small pebbles (around 49 to 70 stones) from the ground, which are used the next day for the Rami al-Jamarat ritual — the symbolic stoning of Satan at the three stone pillars in Mina. The plain is also known as al-Mashar al-Haram (the Sacred Monument), and it holds deep spiritual significance as a place of transition between the profound devotion of Arafat and the active rituals of Mina.
sites.significance: Essential Hajj pilgrimage site; overnight resting place between Arafat and Mina; pilgrims collect pebbles here for the Jamarat stoning ritual
sites.architecturalStyle: Open plain with modern pilgrim infrastructure

sites.name: Mount Thawr
sites.shortDescription: A mountain south of Makkah containing the Cave of Thawr, where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and Abu Bakr (RA) took refuge during the Hijrah.
sites.fullDescription: Mount Thawr (Jabal Thawr) is a mountain located approximately 5 kilometres south of Makkah, Saudi Arabia. It is most renowned for the Cave of Thawr (Ghar Thawr), a small cavern near the summit where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and his closest companion Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) hid for three days during the historic Hijrah (migration) from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE. The Quraysh of Makkah had placed a bounty on the Prophet's head and were actively searching for him. Allah caused a spider to weave a web across the entrance of the cave and a dove to build a nest and lay eggs there, leading the pursuers to believe no one could have entered recently. This divine protection is referenced in the Quran: "If you do not aid the Prophet – Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved had driven him out [of Makkah] as one of two, when they were in the cave and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." [Surah At-Tawbah 9:40]. The mountain and cave remain a powerful symbol of divine protection, trust in Allah, and the steadfast friendship between the Prophet and Abu Bakr. Today, the site is visited by pilgrims and visitors who climb the mountain to see the cave and reflect on this pivotal moment in Islamic history.
sites.significance: Site of the Cave of Thawr — divine refuge of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and Abu Bakr (RA) during the Hijrah; symbol of trust in Allah and the steadfast bond between the Prophet and his companion

sites.name: Mount Hira
sites.shortDescription: A mountain north of Makkah containing the Cave of Hira, where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) received the first revelation of the Quran.
sites.fullDescription: Mount Hira (Jabal al-Nour, the Mountain of Light) is a mountain located approximately 3 kilometres northeast of Makkah, Saudi Arabia, rising to about 642 metres above sea level. At its summit lies the Cave of Hira (Ghar Hira), a small cavern approximately 3.7 metres long and 1.6 metres wide. This cave holds the singular distinction of being the place where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) received the very first revelation of the Quran through the Angel Jibreel (Gabriel). The Prophet would regularly retreat to this cave for meditation and reflection, spending the month of Ramadan in solitude. It was during one such retreat in the month of Ramadan, in the year 610 CE, when the Angel Jibreel appeared to him and commanded him to "Read!" (Iqra), delivering the first verses of Surah Al-Alaq (96:1-5). This moment marks the beginning of the Prophetic mission and the revelation of the Quran, the central miracle of Islam. The mountain is known as Jabal al-Nour (Mountain of Light) because of the profound spiritual illumination that emanated from this event. Today, thousands of visitors climb the steep path of approximately 1,200 steps to reach the cave, seeking to connect with the place where the Divine Word first touched the heart of the Final Messenger. The climb is challenging but deeply meaningful, and the view of Makkah from the summit is breathtaking.
sites.significance: The Cave of Hira — sacred site where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) received the first revelation of the Quran through Angel Jibreel; birthplace of the Prophetic mission

sites.name: Ghars Well
sites.shortDescription: One of Madinah's most renowned prophetic wells, blessed by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
sites.fullDescription: Ghars Well is one of Madinah's most renowned prophetic wells, holding profound spiritual significance in Islamic history. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) drank from its waters, performed ablution with it, and prayed for its blessing. He also instructed the noble Companion Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) to use its water for washing him after his passing. The well was dug by Malik ibn Al-Nahhat, the ancestor of Saad ibn Khaythmah, who owned the well during the Prophet's migration to Madinah. When the Prophet arrived in Madinah, he stayed nearby at Saad's house. He drank from the well, performed ablution, prayed over its waters, and poured in honey gifted to him, enhancing its purity and blessing. Over time, it became a symbol of divine grace and spiritual nourishment. The name "Ghars" refers to a young plant or seedling, reflecting the well's location in a historic palm garden. Ghars Well is one of the seven prophetic wells still preserved in Madinah. The government of Saudi Arabia has maintained and restored the site as part of its heritage and pilgrim services, ensuring that visitors can witness its historical and spiritual significance. The well is located in the Al-Awali district, Quba area, approximately 1.5 kilometres northeast of Quba Mosque.
sites.significance: One of the seven prophetic wells of Madinah; blessed by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH); water used for his final washing

sites.name: Mount Uhud
sites.shortDescription: The mountain north of Madinah where the Battle of Uhud was fought, and where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was injured.
sites.fullDescription: Mount Uhud (Jabal Uhud) is a mountain located approximately 5 kilometres north of Madinah, Saudi Arabia. It is one of the most significant sites in early Islamic history as the location of the Battle of Uhud, which took place in the year 3 AH (625 CE). This was the second major battle between the Muslims of Madinah and the Quraysh of Makkah. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) personally led the Muslim forces of approximately 700 fighters against the Quraysh army of 3,000. During the battle, the Prophet was injured when his helmet was crushed by a chain-mail link, and his uncle Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib (RA), the Lion of Allah, was martyred. The mountain holds the graves of the 70 martyrs of Uhud, including Hamza (RA), and remains a place of deep reverence for Muslims worldwide. The Prophet expressed his love for this mountain, saying: "Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it." Visitors to Madinah often make the journey to Mount Uhud to pay respects at the martyrs' cemetery and to reflect on the lessons of faith, patience, and sacrifice that the battle embodies. The site serves as a powerful reminder of the early struggles of the Muslim community and the ultimate triumph of perseverance.
sites.significance: Site of the Battle of Uhud; graves of 70 martyrs including Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib (RA); mountain loved by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)

sites.name: Masjid Ayesha
sites.shortDescription: A mosque near the boundary of Makkah used as the miqat for local residents performing Umrah.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid Ayesha, also known as Masjid Taneem or Masjid Umrah, is a mosque located at the boundary of the Haram area in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, near the neighbourhood of Taneem. It serves as the designated miqat (boundary point for entering the sacred state of Ihram) for residents of Makkah and those already within the Haram area who wish to perform Umrah. Pilgrims visiting Masjid Ayesha enter Ihram here before returning to Makkah to perform the Tawaf and Sa'i rituals of Umrah. The mosque is named after Ayesha bint Abu Bakr (RA), the Mother of the Believers, who asked the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) whether she could perform Umrah on behalf of others. The Prophet instructed her brother Abdur Rahman to accompany her to the boundary of Makkah (Taneem) to enter Ihram, establishing this location as the miqat for those already within Makkah. The mosque has been expanded over the years to accommodate the large number of pilgrims who use it daily, and it remains one of the most visited sites in Makkah for local Umrah performers.
sites.significance: Miqat for local residents of Makkah performing Umrah; named after Ayesha bint Abu Bakr (RA)

sites.name: Miqat Yalamlam
sites.shortDescription: A miqat point for pilgrims travelling from Yemen and the south to perform Hajj or Umrah.
sites.fullDescription: Yalamlam is a valley located approximately 100 kilometres south of Makkah, Saudi Arabia. It serves as the designated miqat (boundary point for entering the sacred state of Ihram) for pilgrims travelling from Yemen, the southern Arabian Peninsula, and those approaching Makkah from the south. At Yalamlam, pilgrims must enter the state of Ihram before continuing to Makkah to perform Hajj or Umrah. The valley is mentioned in hadith literature as one of the five designated miqats established by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) for pilgrims approaching from different directions. The other miqats are Dhul-Hulayfah (for Madinah), Al-Juhfah (for the Levant and Egypt), Qarn al-Manazil (for Najd and Taif), and Dhat Irq (for Iraq). Yalamlam's location in the mountainous terrain of the southern Hijaz made it a natural boundary point for caravans travelling from Yemen, historically one of the most important pilgrimage routes. Today, modern roads connect Yalamlam to Makkah, but the site remains an essential stop for pilgrims from the south to assume Ihram and make their intentions for the sacred pilgrimage.
sites.significance: Miqat for pilgrims from Yemen and the southern Arabian Peninsula; one of the five designated boundary points for entering Ihram

sites.name: Miqat Dhat Irq
sites.shortDescription: A miqat point for pilgrims travelling from Iraq, Iran, and the northeast to perform Hajj or Umrah.
sites.fullDescription: Miqat Dhat Irq is a valley located approximately 90 kilometres northeast of Makkah, Saudi Arabia. It serves as the designated miqat (boundary point for entering the sacred state of Ihram) for pilgrims travelling from Iraq, Iran, and the northeastern regions of the Arabian Peninsula. At Dhat Irq, pilgrims must enter the state of Ihram before continuing to Makkah to perform Hajj or Umrah. The site is mentioned in hadith literature as one of the five designated miqats established by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) for pilgrims approaching from different directions. The other miqats are Dhul-Hulayfah (for Madinah), Al-Juhfah (for the Levant and Egypt), Qarn al-Manazil (for Najd and Taif), and Yalamlam (for Yemen). Dhat Irq's location in the eastern mountains made it a natural boundary point for caravans travelling from the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia. The site features a mosque and facilities for pilgrims to prepare for Ihram, including changing rooms and prayer areas. Today, it remains an essential stop for pilgrims arriving from Iraq and Iran, who use the nearby Taif road to reach Makkah.
sites.significance: Miqat for pilgrims from Iraq, Iran, and the northeast; one of the five designated boundary points for entering Ihram

sites.name: Al Fuqayr Well
sites.shortDescription: A prophetic well in Madinah tied to the story of Salman al-Farisi (RA) and the miracle of the 300 palm trees.
sites.fullDescription: Al Fuqayr Well is one of Madinah's most significant heritage sites, deeply connected to the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and the story of the noble Companion Salman al-Farisi (RA). Located in the Al-Shuraybat district of Madinah, near Salman al-Farisi's mosque and farm, the well draws from underground water linked to Wadi Bathan. It stands as a living symbol of faith, work, and divine blessing. The well takes its name from the nearby farm tied to Salman al-Farisi's story of freedom. His master agreed to grant him liberty in exchange for 300 fruitful palm trees. The Prophet (PBUH) invited his companions to help plant them, leaving one tree unplanted. The Prophet then said, "Go and dig for it," and planted it himself. By Allah's will, that palm took root and flourished within the same year — a moment of faith and miracle that gave the well its lasting blessing. The land surrounding Al Fuqayr Well once belonged to a Companion martyred in the Battle of Uhud, who had dedicated his wealth as charity. The Prophet (PBUH) used part of this land, including the well and its farm, as one of Islam's earliest charitable endowments (waqf). Today, the Government of Saudi Arabia preserves and restores the site as part of its mission to safeguard Madinah's prophetic landmarks. The well is approximately 4 kilometres southwest of the Prophet's Mosque, making it an easily reachable stop for visitors to the holy city.
sites.significance: Tied to the story of Salman al-Farisi (RA) and the miracle of 300 palm trees; one of Islam's earliest charitable endowments (waqf); blessed by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)

sites.name: Bani Unaif Mosque
sites.shortDescription: One of the earliest mosques in Madinah where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) prayed, built by the Bani Unaif tribe in the 2nd year AH.
sites.fullDescription: On the northern outskirts of Madinah, within the historic dwellings of the Bani Unaif tribe, stands a mosque that preserves the trace of a noble visit by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). Its story dates back to the second year after the Hijrah, when the Prophet (PBUH) visited his companion Talhah ibn Al-Bara ibn Ubayr ibn Wabra (RA), a young man from the Bani Unaif tribe who had fallen ill. During this visit, the Prophet (PBUH) prayed near one of their forts, and the tribe carefully preserved the place where he prayed. They sprinkled the ground with water to protect its mark until they built a mosque over it, a lasting symbol of love, reverence, and devotion. The original structure of Masjid Bani Unaif was modest in scale and design, covering around 35 square meters. It consisted of four basalt stone walls about two meters high and sixty centimeters thick, with no roof. At its center was a simple mihrab framed by neatly hewn basalt stones, and its entrance faced north. This straightforward form reflected the humility of early Islamic architecture in Madinah — purposeful, enduring, and built purely for worship. In recognition of its deep spiritual and historical value, the Saudi government undertook a careful restoration of Bani Unaif mosque in 1442 AH (2020 CE), preserving its original stonework while enhancing its structural integrity. The restoration works included reinforcing the original basalt walls with supporting arches inspired by traditional Madinah architecture, installing a wooden-covered iron roof structure for protection and stability, and creating a landscaped courtyard surrounded by a stone wall adorned with heritage-style arches. Further site improvements were completed in 1445 AH (2024 CE), providing visitor parking and upgraded access routes around the mosque. It stands among the earliest mosques where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) prayed, a symbol of the Prophet's kindness, connection, and compassion toward his companions and the people of Madinah, and an authentic representation of the city's early mosque architecture.
sites.significance: One of the earliest mosques where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) prayed; built by the Bani Unaif tribe to preserve the blessed spot of his prayer; restored in 2020 CE

sites.name: Masjid Ghamama
sites.shortDescription: A historic mosque in Madinah where a cloud once shaded the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) during prayer.
sites.fullDescription: Masjid Ghamama, also known as Masjid al-Ghamamah, is a historic mosque located in Madinah, Saudi Arabia, near the Jannat al-Baqi' cemetery and northwest of Masjid An-Nabawi. The mosque derives its name from the Arabic word "ghamamah" meaning cloud, referring to the miraculous event when a cloud shaded the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) while he was praying at this location. This divine shade protected him from the intense heat of the Arabian sun, and the spot was later commemorated with a mosque. The mosque holds special significance as one of the historical mosques in Madinah associated with the Prophet's prayers and presence. The original structure was modest, built from local materials, and it has been restored and maintained over the centuries. The current building preserves the sanctity of the location while accommodating visitors who come to pray and reflect on this blessed spot. The mosque is part of the rich tapestry of prophetic landmarks in Madinah that preserve the memory of the Prophet Muhammad's life and the early Muslim community.
sites.significance: Historic mosque where a cloud miraculously shaded the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) during prayer; one of Madinah's prophetic landmarks

sites.name: Masjid Abu Bakr As-Siddiq
sites.shortDescription: A historic mosque in the Musalla area of Madinah where the Prophet (PBUH) performed Eid prayers, named after Abu Bakr As-Siddiq.
sites.fullDescription: This mosque was built in the Musalla area at one of the locations where the Prophet (peace be upon him) performed the Eid prayer. Historical accounts suggest that Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq prayed Eid at this spot during his caliphate, leading to its association with his name. For nearly two centuries — the 7th and 8th AH — it served as the principal Eid prayer area for the people of Madinah. The first construction of the mosque was initiated by Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz during his governorship of Madinah (86–93 AH / 705–712 CE). Over the centuries it witnessed multiple renovations, and its current structure dates back to 1254 AH (1838 CE). In the modern Saudi era, the mosque has received exceptional care, including restoration and preservation of its traditional character, ensuring it remains a living testament to the unity of worshippers gathered around the legacy of the Prophet (peace be upon him) during Eid.
sites.significance: Historic Eid prayer site in Madinah associated with Abu Bakr As-Siddiq; built in the Prophet Musalla area

sites.name: Masjid Ali bin Abi Talib
sites.shortDescription: A historic mosque in the Musalla area of Madinah built on a site where the Prophet (PBUH) performed Eid prayers, named after Ali ibn Abi Talib.
sites.fullDescription: This mosque was built on one of the sites where the Prophet (peace be upon him) performed the Eid prayer. It was named after Ali ibn Abi Talib because he led the Eid prayer at this location during the caliphate of Uthman — hence its association with his name. Another view suggests the name was chosen simply to distinguish it from the other Musalla mosques. The first construction dates back to the governorship of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (86–93 AH / 705–712 CE). The mosque has undergone several restorations throughout history. In the modern Saudi era, it was rebuilt in 1411 AH (1991 CE) and received further enhancement during the reign of King Salman bin Abdulaziz, with careful preservation of its historic architectural character — ensuring it remains a prominent landmark connected to the Prophetic Musalla.
sites.significance: Historic Eid prayer site in Madinah associated with Ali ibn Abi Talib; rebuilt in modern Saudi era while preserving traditional character

sites.name: Masjid Umar ibn Al-Khattab
sites.shortDescription: A historic mosque in the southern Musalla area of Madinah, built near the site of the Prophet third Eid prayer.
sites.fullDescription: This mosque was built in the southern part of the Musalla area after 850 AH (1446 CE) by Shaykh Shams al-Din Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Salawi. It became popularly known as Umar Mosque, a name that has endured to the present day. Its current structure dates back to the 13th century AH. Many historians believe it was constructed on or near the site of the house of Abdullah ibn Dhurah al-Muzani — the location where the Prophet (peace be upon him) performed his third Eid prayer. They suggest that this house was situated southwest of Al-Musalla Mosque, close to the current location of the mosque. In the Saudi era, the mosque has received extensive care, including restoration, maintenance, and development works that preserved its architectural and historical significance, allowing it to stand as a witness to one of the notable sites of the Prophetic Eid prayers in Madinah.
sites.significance: Historic Eid prayer site in Madinah believed to be near the Prophet third Eid prayer location; restored in modern Saudi era

sites.name: The Seven Mosques
sites.shortDescription: A complex of seven small mosques located at the site of the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq) in Madinah.
sites.fullDescription: The Seven Mosques (Al-Masajid al-Saba) is a historic site located on the western slope of Mount Sala near the site of the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq) in Madinah, Saudi Arabia. The complex consists of seven small mosques, each built at a historically significant location. The most prominent is the Al-Fath Mosque (Mosque of Victory), built at the site where the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) prayed during the Battle of the Trench. Another is the Salman Al-Farisi Mosque, marking the place where Salman Al-Farisi (RA) suggested the trench strategy. The others include the Abu Bakr Mosque, Umar Mosque, Ali Mosque, Saad ibn Muadh Mosque, and Fatimah Mosque. The Battle of the Trench (5 AH / 627 CE) was a decisive military engagement where the Muslims of Madinah, under the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), defended the city against a coalition of Arab and Jewish tribes. The trench strategy, suggested by the Persian companion Salman Al-Farisi (RA), was a revolutionary defensive tactic that had never been used in Arabian warfare before. The coalition forces, numbering approximately 10,000, were unable to cross the trench and eventually withdrew after a month-long siege. The site remains a powerful reminder of the Prophet strategic genius, the unity of the early Muslim community, and the divine support that protected Madinah. In the modern Saudi era, the site has been preserved and enhanced as a heritage landmark, with the mosques maintained and the surrounding area developed to accommodate visitors who come to reflect on this pivotal moment in Islamic history.
sites.significance: Site of the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq); seven historic mosques marking key locations of the Prophet defensive strategy and the trench plan of Salman Al-Farisi (RA)

sites.name: Imam Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab Mosque
sites.arabicName: مسجد الإمام محمد بن عبد الوهاب
sites.shortDescription: Qatar's national grand mosque, named after the 18th-century reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.
sites.fullDescription: Inaugurated in 2011 as the State Mosque of Qatar, the Imam Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab Mosque is the largest mosque in the country. Built in the traditional Najdi architectural style with sand-coloured limestone, it features 93 domes covering the prayer hall, three large central domes, and a single elegant minaret. The complex spans roughly 175,000 m² with an indoor capacity of about 12,000 worshippers and accommodates 30,000 including the courtyards. It is named after Sheikh Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792), the influential Najdi religious scholar.
sites.significance: National grand mosque of Qatar; one of the largest mosques in the Gulf region

sites.name: Ibrahim Al Khaleel Masjid
sites.shortDescription: Community mosque in Doha named for the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), 'the Friend of God'.
sites.fullDescription: Located in northern Doha, Masjid Ibrahim Al Khaleel takes its name from one of the honorific titles of the Prophet Ibrahim — 'Al-Khaleel' (the Friend of God, Khalīl Allāh). The mosque serves the surrounding neighbourhood with daily and Jumu'ah prayers, Qur'an programmes, and Ramadan tarawih. Its design draws on contemporary Gulf mosque architecture with a central dome and pair of slender minarets.
sites.significance: Active neighbourhood mosque in Doha dedicated to the legacy of Prophet Ibrahim

sites.name: Islamic Cultural Center of New York
sites.shortDescription: The first mosque purpose-built in New York City, on Manhattan's Upper East Side.
sites.fullDescription: Inaugurated in 1991 on East 96th Street and Third Avenue, the Islamic Cultural Center of New York was the first mosque purpose-built in New York City. Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, its modernist form is precisely rotated to face Mecca, slightly off the Manhattan street grid. A single 130-foot minaret and a copper-clad dome rise above the prayer hall, which holds around 1,000 worshippers. The center serves NYC's diverse Muslim community and includes a school and meeting halls.
sites.significance: First purpose-built mosque in New York City; flagship Islamic institution in the Northeast US

sites.name: Masjid Al-Farooq
sites.shortDescription: Atlanta's largest mosque, named for Umar ibn Al-Khattab (Al-Farooq).
sites.fullDescription: Al-Farooq Masjid of Atlanta sits at 442 14th Street NW in Midtown Atlanta and is one of the largest mosques in the Southeastern United States. Originally founded in 1980 in a converted house, the community completed its current purpose-built structure in 2008. The mosque features a distinctive turquoise central dome, twin minarets, and a striking modern Islamic facade in white stone. Its name honours the second caliph, Umar ibn Al-Khattab, who bore the title 'Al-Farooq' (the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood).
sites.significance: Largest mosque in the Southeastern United States; major center for Atlanta's Muslim community

sites.name: East Plano Islamic Center
sites.shortDescription: EPIC — one of the largest mosques in Texas, serving the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.
sites.fullDescription: The East Plano Islamic Center (EPIC) is a major mosque and community campus in Plano, Texas. Established to serve the rapidly growing Muslim community of the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, EPIC offers daily and Jumu'ah prayers, a full-time Islamic school, youth programmes, and large Ramadan and Eid gatherings. Its modern architecture combines a large central dome with a contemporary American Islamic civic style.
sites.significance: One of the largest mosques in Texas and a hub for the North Texas Muslim community

hotspots.label: The Kaaba
hotspots.description: The Kaaba is a cube-shaped structure at the center of Masjid Al-Haram. Muslims believe it was first built by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Ismail. Covered in black silk embroidered with gold Quranic verses (the Kiswa), it is the most sacred point in Islam. Muslims circumambulate (tawaf) around the Kaaba during Hajj and Umrah.
hotspots.historicalPeriod: Originally built by Prophet Ibrahim; rebuilt multiple times

hotspots.label: Black Stone
hotspots.description: The Black Stone (Al-Hajar al-Aswad) is set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba. Islamic tradition holds that it fell from paradise and was originally pure white, darkening over centuries. Pilgrims attempt to touch or kiss it when possible. It is framed in a silver holder and marks the starting point for circumambulation of the Kaaba.
hotspots.historicalPeriod: Pre-Islamic; mentioned in hadith of the Prophet

hotspots.label: Zamzam Well
hotspots.description: The Zamzam Well is a miraculous well located within the Masjid Al-Haram compound. According to Islamic tradition, it was miraculously created by Allah for Hagar (Hajar) and her infant son Ismail when they were left in the desert. The well has supplied water for over 4,000 years. Pilgrims drink Zamzam water as a religious practice.
hotspots.historicalPeriod: Over 4,000 years old; Islamic tradition traces to Prophet Ibrahim's time

hotspots.label: Golden Dome
hotspots.description: The magnificent golden dome of the Dome of the Rock is 20 metres in diameter and 25 metres in height. Originally covered in gold, it was later covered in lead and then aluminum. In 1993, Jordan's King Hussein donated 80 kg of gold to restore its golden appearance. The dome sits on a drum decorated with elaborate tile inscriptions.
hotspots.historicalPeriod: Original dome: 691 CE; golden covering restored: 1993 CE

hotspots.label: Foundation Stone
hotspots.description: The Foundation Stone (al-Sakhrah al-Musharrafah) is the rock beneath the dome, one of the holiest sites in three Abrahamic faiths. In Islam, it is believed to be the spot from which Prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven during the Night Journey. It measures approximately 18 by 13 metres and is enclosed by a wooden screen.
hotspots.historicalPeriod: Pre-Islamic; site of Prophet's ascension during Isra wal Miraj (621 CE)

hotspots.label: Byzantine Mosaics
hotspots.description: The interior of the Dome of the Rock is adorned with spectacular Byzantine-style mosaics covering over 280 metres in the upper drum and arcade. Dating to the Umayyad period (691 CE), these mosaics feature intricate floral and jewel motifs without human figures, consistent with Islamic artistic tradition. They represent the finest surviving example of early Islamic decorative arts.

hotspots.label: Striped Arches
hotspots.description: The distinctive red-and-white voussoir arches of the Great Mosque of Cordoba are its most iconic architectural feature. This double-arch system was an innovative structural solution that allowed the builders to raise the ceiling height beyond what a single arch could support. The alternating red brick and white limestone creates a visually stunning rhythmic pattern.

hotspots.label: The Mihrab
hotspots.description: The mihrab of the Great Mosque of Cordoba is considered one of the most beautiful mihrabs in the Islamic world. Constructed in 965 CE under Caliph Al-Hakam II, it is a masterpiece of Umayyad art. The horseshoe arch entrance is framed by elaborate marble columns and Byzantine-style mosaics commissioned from the Byzantine Emperor. The interior of the mihrab is a small octagonal chamber.

hotspots.label: Forest of Columns
hotspots.description: The prayer hall of the Great Mosque contains over 850 columns of jasper, onyx, marble, and granite, creating a hypnotic 'forest' effect. Many columns were reused from earlier Roman and Visigothic structures. The regular grid of columns creates an infinite repetition of arches in every direction, producing a meditative visual effect that has inspired architects for over a millennium.

hotspots.label: Court of the Lions
hotspots.description: The Court of the Lions is the most celebrated space in the Alhambra, built by Emir Muhammad V in the 14th century. It features a central marble fountain supported by twelve sculpted lions, from which four channels of water radiate outward. The surrounding gallery features 124 slender marble columns with intricately carved muqarnas capitals. The fountain represents the Garden of Paradise.

hotspots.label: Muqarnas Ceiling
hotspots.description: The muqarnas ceiling of the Hall of the Abencerrages is one of the most spectacular architectural features in the Alhambra. Muqarnas are stalactite-like three-dimensional decorative vaulting elements used extensively in Islamic architecture. This ceiling contains over 5,000 individual plaster cells arranged in concentric rings, creating a breathtaking honeycomb effect that seems to dissolve into infinity.

hotspots.label: Arabesque Stucco
hotspots.description: The walls of the Alhambra are covered in intricate stucco arabesque panels featuring flowing geometric patterns, vegetal motifs, and calligraphic inscriptions from the Quran and Nasrid poetry. The famous Nasrid motto 'There is no victor but Allah' (Wa la ghalib illa Allah) is repeated throughout. These stucco panels were originally brilliantly painted in red, blue, gold, and other colors.
